F001.why: Most statements value the student's own voice and originality (Denver, UPR Rio Piedras, Wayne State, Georgia Tech) rather than banning AI; only Montana State reads as a ban.

F002.why: The point is what counts when work is evaluated: UPR 'esenciales para la evaluación del aprendizaje', Montana State 'Only content done by a student ... is accepted'.

F003.value: Instructors should assign writing in writing-intensive courses to be done without AI.
F003.why: Both Bucknell statements are about assigning AI-free writing in W courses, not about grading.

F004.why: All three statements (UND, UTHSC, Michigan State) are about doubting vendor claims, which takes no position on AI use.

F005.why: Stony Brook 'if and only if the instructor permits it' and Southern Mississippi 'faculty must approve its use' leave the decision to the instructor.

F006.why: Both Stony Brook statements set a procedural approval step for any individual policy, whatever its stance on AI.

F007.why: Most statements ask instructors to state that unauthorized use is misconduct (Iowa, Delaware, Idaho, VCU, Notre Dame), which holds whatever the course allows; UND applies it to restrict or ban policies alike.

F008.why: The instructor decides whether uploading is allowed: UC Santa Cruz 'whether you will allow them', Penn 'you may wish to set a policy', Nova Southeastern 'you may consider allowing'.

F009.value: Let your students opt out of AI-assisted grading and request human review of their work.
F009.why: The duty is the instructor's: Nebraska Omaha 'Instructors should offer a human-alternative', Utah 'Students must be able to opt out ... without penalty', Georgia State 'must have a right to request human review'.

F010.why: Most statements are general ethics and standards duties (Davidson, Hampton, NDSU, USF, Rochester, Wake Forest); the restrictive items come mainly from Oregon State.

F011.value: Tell students when you use AI on their work, and get their permission before putting their work into AI tools.
F011.why: Statements split between disclosure (Appalachian State 'Disclose', Maine 'inform students', Utah State 'inform students') and consent (Nebraska Omaha, Purdue, Appalachian opt-in, TWU opt out); the current wording drops disclosure.

F012.why: Every statement concerns grading or assessment of student work (Georgia State, UNCG, Northeastern, Penn State Senate Policy 47-20, Rochester).

F013.why: The current wording is defensible: UIUC 'rather than using AI-generated replies' and MIT's concern about AI where a human touch is needed support it, while JMU and Wake Forest only add the human-centered framing.

F014.why: Watching drafts, checkpoints and reflections (JMU, UNF, UNC Charlotte) is a teaching duty that takes no position on AI use.

F015.why: Statements ask instructors to choose the exam format (Boise State 'Change all exams to be in-class', Cornell 'moving assessments from take-home to in-class', 'rework the question'), which is assessment design.

F016.why: Responding to misuse (Montana's matrix, UNF sanctions, Oklahoma State consequences, Portland State grade) holds whatever the course's AI stance.

F017.value: Respond to AI misuse with consequences that fit the case, from education or resubmission to failing the assignment, taking account of intent and how clear the policy was.
F017.why: No statement mentions prior offenses; Montana ties responses to intent and policy clarity and Oklahoma State/UNF name failing or forfeiting credit.

F018.value: Instructors should respond to AI misuse in proportion, weighing intent and how clear the rules were.
F018.why: 'Past offenses' appears in none of the six statements; Montana's rules turn on intent and clarity.

F019.value: Instructors should keep AI-assisted work focused on students' own interpretation and critical analysis.
F019.why: Azusa Pacific's only statement is about focusing work on students' interpretation and analysis, nothing about banning.

F020.value: You may allow students to use AI to analyze quantitative or qualitative data.
F020.why: The only statement (UL Lafayette 'Use of GAI to analyze quantitative or qualitative data') names a use, not a duty to define uses.

F021.why: All seven statements are options ('may', 'can'): Yeshiva 'may assist', Cornell 'may have selective utility', Wisconsin 'can assist'.

F022.value: You may use AI to help draft formative feedback, flag patterns in student responses and generate ideas for feedback.
F022.why: None of the seven statements mentions personalizing feedback; they list drafting feedback, flagging patterns and generating ideas.

F023.value: Instructors may use AI to help draft feedback and spot patterns in student work.
F023.why: No statement asks for personalization; all permit AI help with feedback (Yeshiva, South Dakota, UMass Boston, Georgia State).

F024.why: Attending training (Cornell, Gonzaga, Alaska Fairbanks, Missouri integrity sprint, LSU data privacy workshops) is professional development that does not itself invite AI use.

F025.why: Statements set conditions on how AI is used (Florida State 'used in ways that support student learning outcomes and promote transparency', Texas Tech 'prioritize human agency'), which is permission under conditions rather than promotion or no position.

F026.value: When you use AI, use it in ways that support student learning outcomes and transparency, balance academic integrity with its benefits, and prioritize human agency.
F026.why: The statements condition use rather than ask instructors to use AI (Florida State, UTSA, Texas Tech).

F027.value: Instructors should assign tasks where students use AI to learn or critique its output.
F027.why: None of the four statements (Clark, Mines, UNR, NAU) sets an 'own work first' condition; they assign AI for tutoring or exploration.

F028.value: Show students how to use generative AI as a teaching assistant.
F028.why: Alaska Fairbanks's only statement says 'as a teaching assistant' and does not mention code syntax or debugging.

F029.value: Instructors should assign tasks where students use AI to learn or critique its output.
F029.why: Alaska Fairbanks's statement sets no 'own work first' condition.

F030.value: Instructors should assign tasks where students use AI to learn or critique its output.
F030.why: Mines's 'Invite students to use custom AI chatbots' sets no 'own work first' condition.

F031.value: You may use AI to identify errors in student code and suggest possible fixes.
F031.why: Penn State's statement is an option ('AI can help'), matching the choice tag.

F032.value: Spend your effort teaching students to use AI responsibly rather than policing and penalizing AI use.
F032.why: Statements contrast teaching with policing (South Carolina 'Rather than police and penalize', Kansas, UTEP 'not to catch'); none mentions banning.

F033.value: Instructors should teach responsible AI use rather than policing it.
F033.why: 'Banning' appears in none of the four statements; they contrast teaching with policing.

F034.why: Sharing syllabus statements and assignments with colleagues (Prairie View, Smith, Vermont) takes no position on AI use.

F035.why: Assessing impact and adjusting (VCU 'Regularly assess the impact', 'Solicit feedback ... and adjust'; UTSA 'measure the development of foundational skills') is a review duty whatever the stance.

F036.why: Statements ask instructors to align with department and school policy (Alabama, Duquesne, Indiana, Iowa, Maryland), a duty that holds whatever the stance.

F037.why: All four statements grant options: Alabama 'permissible', CU Boulder 'may determine', ETSU 'may also establish', Jackson State 'may have additional criteria'.

F038.why: Hundreds of statements ask instructors to state clearly whether and how AI is allowed, which applies whatever they decide (Vanderbilt 'even if you choose to completely prohibit').

F039.why: Statements ask for assignment-level communication of AI rules (Augusta, American, JMU, Oregon), a communication duty whatever the stance.

F040.why: Co-creating rules needs students present and is placed at the start: UCLA 'at the beginning of the quarter', JMU 'in week one', Montana State 'initial discussion'.

F041.value: Instructors should disclose to students whether and how they use generative AI.
F041.why: All statements are about instructors disclosing AI use in their own course materials (Penn, URI, Cornell, Oregon State), not co-writing a policy.

F042.value: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy.
F042.why: Statements ask for a definition of AI in the policy (Austin CC, ETSU, Kentucky); none involves students in writing it.

F043.value: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy.
F043.why: Statements concern the tone and wording of the instructor's policy (Carleton, UC Santa Cruz, Kentucky); none involves co-writing with students.

F044.value: Instructors should write a clear, ethical course AI policy.
F044.why: Both statements ask only for a syllabus notice on ethical, responsible AI use.

F045.value: Instructors should make ethical and responsible use central when they bring AI into their courses.
F045.why: Neither statement is about writing a policy or involving students: Florida State 'Ethical use should be a primary consideration when making decisions about implementing AI'; Nebraska Omaha 'Ensure AI integration in your class promotes ethical and responsible use'.

F046.value: Instructors should decide and state what records of AI use and of their own work students must keep or submit.
F046.why: All statements concern documentation requirements (Mercer, Howard, UCLA, Wisconsin transcripts), not AI-resistant redesign.

F047.value: Instructors should state in the rubric whether and how AI use counts in grading.
F047.why: Most statements put AI use into rubrics or grading criteria (Austin CC, Azusa Pacific, Clark Atlanta, UCCS, Boston University baselines); only Boise State is about making AI shortcuts a detriment.

F048.value: Instructors should select or develop AI tools that preserve usage data.
F048.why: Rochester's only statement is about tool choice, not penalties.

F049.value: Instructors should collect an early in-person writing sample to know each student's own writing.
F049.why: Statements ask for a baseline writing sample (UC Santa Cruz, Nebraska-Lincoln, Seton Hall, Denver), not for announcing detection or penalties.

F050.value: Instructors should remind students that they are responsible for the work they submit, including any AI content in it.
F050.why: Statements are about student accountability for submitted work (Arizona, Florida, Virginia, NIU), with nothing on detection or punishment.

F051.why: Statements choose assessment conditions and formats (Texas Tech timed assignments, West Florida question banks, UTRGV time limits, CUNY shorter in-class work), which is assessment design.

F052.why: Statements ask for reminders and discussions throughout the semester and before assignments (Harvey Mudd, Delaware, CUNY, Smith), not revising policy.

F053.why: William & Mary's statement is about reviewing submitted work for AI-generated content as needed, i.e. detection.

F054.why: The full CS 2340 sentence (checked in the course packet) reserves the right to ask for worklogs and prompt transcripts at the AI-encouraged level 'to ensure significant learning', not upon suspected misuse.

F055.why: Every statement leaves permission to the instructor: TCU 'except as explicitly authorized by the instructor', Grinnell 'unless stated otherwise by your instructor', San Jose State, Prairie View.

F056.why: All three East Texas A&M statements give the decision to the individual instructor ('Individual instructors may disallow entirely').
